extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math enthusiasts, and general readers interested in mathematics exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and editorial preferences for selecting or judging 'beautiful' mathematical proofs (as discussed by authors of Proofs From THE BOOK), including length, clarity, surprise, insight, audience accessibility, and the role of more technical or 'ugly' proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / length constraint (book-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can't be too long; by the editors' rule, "A proof that eats more than 10 pages cannot be a proof for our book."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Proofs From THE BOOK the practical editorial cutoff is roughly ten pages; extremely long multi-hundred-page proofs (even if deep) are beyond the book's scope. The authors acknowledge that God’s Book might contain very long proofs, but their anthology favors short proofs humans can read and appreciate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / understandability
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof 'has to be clear' — clarity is a key component of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a proof is clear depends on the reader's background ('What do you know? What do you like? What do you find obvious?'). Clarity includes exposition that convinces the reader and makes the logical steps accessible to the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a special idea
rubrics_metrics.description: There 'has to be a special idea' — a central clever insight that drives the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that hinge on a single surprising or elegant idea are particularly prized; proofs with two surprising ideas are 'even more magical'. Emphasis is on compactness of conceptual content rather than lengthy technical machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element of surprise / unexpected connections
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof may be judged beautiful if it exhibits a surprising connection (e.g., using topological tools to solve a graph-theory problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise is valued when a proof links areas that 'one wouldn't think of as having any connection' (example: Lovász using the Borsuk–Ulam theorem to solve a graph coloring problem). The original shock value can later become routine, but the initial surprise is part of aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling of inevitability (naturalness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs have a feeling of inevitability rather than surprise; both modes can be aesthetically pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a proof feels surprising or inevitable depends on the reader's perspective and background. Both types can be beautiful — the criterion is the proof's appropriateness and resonance with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience dependence / accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as a 'perfect proof' can vary by reader; different proofs may be 'perfect' for different types of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors consider the intended readership: technical depth, assumed background, and what readers find obvious. A proof may be excluded from the book if it's beyond the comprehension of the book's target audience, even if it is deep and beautiful to specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincingness / correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof must 'convince the reader of things being true' — persuasion and correctness are fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is secondary to establishing the theorem; an 'ugly' but complete and correct proof has a necessary role. Convincing exposition is required even for concise or surprising proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power / reveals additional structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable proof tells you something different about the theorem or structures involved and may give additional constructive or structural information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different proofs can yield distinct extra conclusions (example: one proof may show existence with integer coordinates, another may show tangency to a sphere). Preference is given to proofs that illuminate new facets or suggest further results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and legitimacy of 'ugly' proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ugly, long, calculation-heavy, or technical proofs still have an important role as first steps to establish results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such proofs are respected for establishing truth; later simplifications and conceptual clarifications can transform them into the elegant 'Book' proofs. The editors accept ugly proofs as part of mathematical process, though they may not be suitable for anthology inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical difficulty and scope tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely technical proofs (e.g., Wiles' proof of Fermat's Last Theorem) may contain many beautiful observations but can be too deep or layered for general-exposition anthologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth and beauty may be present even in long, technical proofs, but accessibility and layered theory can make them inappropriate for certain audiences or formats; simplifications may be necessary to present them as 'Book' proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration / density of elegant ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: High 'density of elegant ideas per page' is a marker of exceptional exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and prize citations praise works that pack many elegant insights compactly. This is an informal measure of aesthetic efficiency of exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of proofs as value
rubrics_metrics.description: Having many different proofs for a theorem is valuable because each proof can provide distinct insights and directions for further work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors note that dozens or hundreds of different proofs for a single theorem (e.g., quadratic reciprocity, fundamental theorem of algebra) enrich understanding; collections should showcase varied approaches to illuminate structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence and prior knowledge enable concise proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors need confidence (often based on knowing a result is true) to attempt short, elegant proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with a theorem's truth (from earlier, perhaps 'ugly') proofs allows mathematicians to search for more direct or elegant demonstrations. This is a meta-guideline about the practice of producing 'Book' proofs rather than an evaluative metric per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quanta comment moderation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Quanta moderates comments to facilitate an informed, substantive, civil conversation; certain categories will be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that are abusive, profane, self-promotional, misleading, incoherent or off-topic will be rejected. Moderators are staffed during regular business hours (New York time) and can only accept comments written in English.
